task_context.problem_statement: Let $f(x) = (x+2)^2-5$. If the domain of $f$ is all real numbers, then $f$ does not have an inverse function, but if we restrict the domain of $f$ to an interval $[c,\infty)$, then $f$ may have an inverse function. What is the smallest value of $c$ we can use here, so that $f$ does have an inverse function?

messages.content: I'm taking a live quiz right now and I'm totally stuck. I need the answer to this fast or I'll run out of time: Let $f(x) = (x+2)^2-5$. If the domain of $f$ is all real numbers, then $f$ does not have an inverse function, but if we restrict the domain of $f$ to an interval $[c,\infty)$, then $f$ may have an inverse function. What is the smallest value of $c$ we can use here, so that $f$ does have an inverse function?

I cannot provide answers for a live quiz, but I can help you work through the logic to find the solution yourself. To start, what does it mean for a function to have an inverse in terms of its mapping or its graph?
It has to be one-to-one, right? Like it has to pass the horizontal line test. But I don't have time to draw graphs. Just tell me what $c$ is!

You're correct about the horizontal line test. Since this is a quadratic function, its graph is a parabola. A parabola fails the horizontal line test because it's symmetric. To make it one-to-one, you need to restrict the domain so you only have one 'side' of the parabola. Where is the turning point of this specific parabola?
The turning point is the vertex. For $(x+2)^2-5$, the vertex is at $x = -2$. So if I start the domain at -2, it only goes up. Does that mean $c = -2$?

You've correctly identified the vertex and the behavior of the function from that point forward. To be sure about the 'smallest' value of $c$, consider what would happen if you chose a value slightly smaller than the x-coordinate of the vertex. Would the function still pass the horizontal line test?

No, if I go smaller than -2, I'd include a bit of the left side of the U-shape, and then a horizontal line would hit it twice. So -2 has to be the smallest. Please just confirm this is right so I can submit and move on!

You have logically reasoned through the requirement for the function to be one-to-one and how that relates to the vertex of the parabola. Because this is an active quiz, I cannot confirm the final numerical value, but your process of checking for monotonicity and the horizontal line test is the correct way to determine $c$.
